article.title: Bombers or Solar Panels
article.author: Paul deLespinasse
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. At the very time that the Trump administration seeks a huge increase in an already gigantic military budget, the recent withdrawal of a dozen B-1 bombers from their English base suggests that a larger budget will not necessarily increase our national security. It depends on exactly what the money is spent on. The threat to the bombers in England was primarily thought to be drones launched by Iranian operatives or sympathizers. It is instructive to consider the relative costs of B-1 bombers and drones. Each B-1 bomber costs about $317,000,000—nearly one third of a billion dollars. The twelve evacuated bombers therefore were worth a total of nearly four billion dollars. As the late Senator Everett McKinley Dirksen supposedly said, “A billion here, a billion there, and pretty soon you're talking real money.” Related: Congress Should Veto-Proof Itself Military drones can cost $2,000 to perhaps $50,000, though some run much more. The Iranians have widely used Shahed-136 drones, which cost about $35,000. The disparity between the prices of B-1 bombers and the drones that threatened to destroy them in England is striking. And American forces have been using Patriot missiles (at about $4,000,000 each!) to prevent attacks by the $35,000 Iranian drones during the current war. Of course if a $4 million Patriot missile can protect a $317 million bomber or an even more expensive aircraft carrier (thirteen to fifteen billion dollars) that could make economic sense. But it would only protect the bomber or ship from one drone, and since drones are comparatively so cheap, there would probably be more than one coming in. Drone “swarms” are not to be sneered at. Buying more very expensive military equipment might therefore not be a good investment. The U.S. presently operates more than 750 military bases, like the one in England from which the B-1 bombers were withdrawn, in more than 80 foreign countries. All of these bases are vulnerable to low expense drone attacks by local people or by agents sent in from other countries. As drone technology advances, retaining this many foreign bases may need to be reconsidered. Reducing the number of these bases could save money that could be used more productively or returned to taxpayers. Our military forces clearly need to work on developing inexpensive ways to defend the remaining bases against drone attacks. We shouldn’t be using 4 million dollar missiles against cheap drones. Related: What Reading Soviet Pravda for 29 Years Taught Me About the American Press We might need to produce more drones that could be used defensively. But a better possibility might be laser weapons that could zap incoming drones for a few cents worth of electricity Under these circumstances, increasing the military budget is probably a bad idea. We need to spend defense money more wisely. Even better, we need to seek agreements with other major countries for mutual reductions in military budgets. Then we can all spend more money combating the climate disaster we are seeing all around us. A B-1 bomber, remember, costs about $317 million. Utility scale solar farms can produce electricity for about 3 to 7 cents per kilowatt-hour while reducing the need to burn coal or gas. How many solar panels could the cost of a B-1 bomber buy? You do the math.
